warnings: AIA.NZ is mid-way through a once-in-a-generation, debt-funded capex supercycle (domestic jet terminal + airfield expansion, guided NZ$1.0-1.6bn/yr capex through the end of the decade, targeted completion ~2029). Reported FCF has been negative every year FY2023-FY2025 (-NZ$247m to -NZ$581m) and is projected to remain deeply negative through roughly FY2030 in this model before turning strongly positive as the capex program tapers to a maintenance level. A rigorous WACC-based DCF that discounts this full negative-then-positive path produces a materially lower intrinsic value than the market price, because Gordon-growth terminal capitalization at a textbook 7-8.5% WACC cannot replicate the ~24.6x EV/EBITDAFI multiple the market currently pays for this regulated monopoly asset (a duration/scarcity premium typical of listed airport infrastructure). This gap is a genuine and important finding, not a modeling error -- it is consistent with the qualitative risk factors already flagged (actual aeronautical returns of 5.53% vs a 7.82% regulatory target, and a recent consensus price-target cut from NZ$9.00 to NZ$8.25, since settling around NZ$8.69). Treat the DCF intrinsic values below as a conservative cash-flow-based floor, and cross-check against the EV/EBITDAFI memo figure and peer/regulatory-asset-base valuation approaches before concluding the stock is overvalued.

SBC is immaterial for AIA.NZ (share-based payments reserve balance of only NZ$2.2m at FY2025, an annual expense of roughly NZ$0.3-0.6m via a small executive long-term incentive share-rights plan covering 8 people) and does not meaningfully affect the valuation or share count.

FY2026 annual results (year ended 30-Jun-2026) are due 20-Aug-2026 and are NOT yet reflected in this model. The latest actuals used are FY2025 (full year) and H1-2026 (half year to 31-Dec-2025). FY26 underlying NPAT guidance (NZ$295-320m) and capex guidance (NZ$1.0-1.2bn) were both issued 19-Feb-2026, before the 2026 Middle East fuel-price shock and June-2026 capacity-driven passenger declines (international -4%, domestic -5% YoY) fully played out; management has not updated guidance since. Re-check this model against the 20-Aug-2026 result before relying on it further.

historical_growth.notes: Reported FCF has been negative every year FY2023-FY2025 (~-NZ$247m to -NZ$581m) due to a once-in-a-generation capex supercycle (domestic jet terminal + airfield expansion, ~NZ$1.0-1.6bn/yr through decade-end vs historical maintenance capex of ~NZ$150-260m). FCF-based CAGRs are not meaningful and are omitted; growth driver for the DCF is revenue (aeronautical volume/price recovery + property rent-roll growth), with owner FCF built from EBITDAFI margin, D&A, tax, capex-guidance and working-capital components rather than extrapolated from history. Equity CAGR is distorted by the Sep-2024 NZ$1.4bn placement/retail equity raise (shares 1472m->1688m) and is not used as the primary growth driver.

base.wacc_rationale: AIA.NZ is a Commerce Commission information-disclosure regulated large-cap NZ infrastructure asset. ComCom's 2026 cost-of-capital determination (5-May-2026, applying the WACC methodology upheld by the High Court's dismissal of the airports' merits-review appeal) is the direct regulatory anchor: airport-sector mid-point vanilla WACC estimates from recent ComCom disclosure years have clustered around 6.5-7.5% nominal post-tax for the regulated aeronautical asset base. The 7.5% base-case WACC sits at the upper end of that regulatory range to reflect that roughly a third of AIA's revenue (retail, car parking, and the growing unregulated property/logistics book) is unregulated and carries a higher required return than the pure aeronautical asset base, plus AIA's elevated leverage (~NZ$2.65bn borrowings, further NZ$1.31bn committed) during the capex supercycle. Bull (7.0%) reflects a scenario where the ComCom-validated regulatory framework and improving credit metrics compress the cost of capital; bear (8.5%) reflects higher-for-longer NZ interest rates and a risk premium for capex execution/regulatory-tightening risk (the live Jan/Mar-2026 Information Disclosure consultation).
base.rationale: Revenue growth decelerates from post-recovery/near-term fuel-shock-affected ~5% (FY26) toward a long-run ~4% (passenger + inflation) by FY35, with a mid-decade bump (FY28-29) as new domestic jet terminal capacity is commissioned. EBITDAFI margin ramps from 69.8% (FY25 actual) toward 73% (mature, PSE5 regulatory reset support). Capex follows management's own guidance of NZ$1.0-1.6bn/yr 'until the end of the decade', peaking ~FY28 as the domestic jet terminal completes (~2029 per the newly finalised 30-Jun-2026 Master Plan), then tapering to a ~NZ$320m/yr (~19% of revenue) maintenance level. The finalised Master Plan explicitly prioritises maximising existing infrastructure ahead of major new construction and sets no build timeline for the safeguarded second-runway land, a capital-discipline signal that modestly supports (but does not by itself lower) the post-FY29 capex taper already assumed here. Cash tax rate held at 27% (close to FY25 effective 24.1% and H1-26 effective 27.5%, near NZ's 28% statutory rate -- no abnormal one-off to ramp away). FY26 near-term growth is not raised despite FY26-YTD passengers still +2%, because June-2026 traffic shows capacity-driven declines (international -4%, domestic -5% YoY) from the Middle East fuel-price shock that are a live headwind into the 20-Aug-2026 FY26 result. SBC held at a flat 0.0597% of revenue throughout (anchored to the corrected FY2025 actual of NZ$0.6m/NZ$1,004.7m) -- immaterial to the model at any plausible path given AIA's tiny 8-person LTI plan.

bull.rationale: Faster international passenger recovery above 2019 levels as the Middle East fuel-price shock fades, successful new route wins (e.g. China Eastern Shanghai-Auckland-Buenos Aires, launched Dec-2025), PSE5 regulatory settings modestly more favourable post the WACC merits-review litigation (High Court dismissed the airports' appeal, providing methodological certainty even if the framework itself is not more generous), and continued property rent-roll outperformance (Manawa Bay, Landing Business Park).

bear.rationale: 2026 Middle East fuel-price shock and airline capacity cuts (Air NZ, Qantas, Emirates, Singapore Airlines) persist longer than expected -- consistent with the June-2026 traffic print already showing international seat capacity -2% and domestic -6% YoY -- PSE4/PSE5 regulatory settings stay unfavourable (actual returns keep lagging the 7.82% target, and the live Jan/Mar-2026 ComCom Information Disclosure and cost-of-capital consultation tightens capex scrutiny further), capex program runs over budget/schedule, and higher-for-longer interest rates raise funding costs on the ~NZ$2.65bn+ debt pile.

bear.note: A negative equity intrinsic value in the bear case is a genuine model output, not an error: it reflects that the ~NZ$1.0-1.6bn/yr capex program is largely already committed/contractual (NZ$1.31bn of PP&E purchase obligations at Dec-2025) and debt-funded, so a scenario combining sustained capacity cuts, weaker margins, and a higher WACC leaves owner FCF unable to service the resulting debt build without either delaying capex, cutting the dividend, or raising further equity. Read as a warning signal (leverage/refinancing risk in a severe downside, reinforced by the June-2026 traffic print already showing capacity-driven passenger declines), not a literal negative per-share value.

valuation_philosophy.summary: This model deliberately values AIA.NZ as a cash-flow-discipline exercise, not as an attempt to reverse-engineer the market price. Owner FCF is built bottom-up from EBITDAFI margin, D&A, tax, management's own capex guidance and working capital over a 10-year explicit horizon -- long enough to carry the debt-funded domestic-terminal-and-airfield capex supercycle (~NZ$1.0-1.6bn/yr, guided through decade-end, ~90% of the airfield programme complete at H1-2026) through its peak (~FY28) and its taper toward a ~NZ$320m/yr maintenance level, consistent with the newly finalised 30-Jun-2026 Master Plan's capital-discipline signal (existing-infrastructure-first, no second-runway build timeline). Discounting that full negative-then-positive path at a large-cap regulated-infrastructure WACC (7.5% base) with a terminal value capped at the lower of Gordon growth or a 20x FCF multiple necessarily produces a base intrinsic value (NZ$1.90) far below the NZ$8.76 market price -- implying roughly a 6-7x EV/EBITDAFI multiple versus AIA's ~17.8x historical trading average (ex-outliers) and ~24.6x current multiple. That gap is not read as a signal the stock is dramatically overvalued; it is read as evidence that the market prices AIA as a scarce, irreplaceable, monopoly-regulated infrastructure asset with a multi-decade duration and optionality (the Master Plan's ~38m passengers/year by the late 2040s, ~2x current volumes) that a textbook WACC-based Gordon DCF structurally cannot capture, particularly while mid-capex-cycle reported and owner FCF are deeply negative. The intended use of this model is therefore as a conservative cash-flow floor and a leverage/execution risk gauge (see the bear case's negative equity value, which flags refinancing risk rather than a literal price), to be read alongside -- not instead of -- the EV/EBITDAFI cross-check and peer/regulated-asset-base valuation approaches. Investors relying purely on this DCF's headline intrinsic value without that context will systematically conclude the stock is far more overvalued than the qualitative and regulatory picture (Commerce Commission-validated capex programme, high-occupancy diversified property book, de facto monopoly position) actually supports.

cross_check_memo.description: Market-implied EV/EBITDAFI multiple cross-check (NOT the primary valuation method). AIA.NZ's regulated-monopoly infrastructure profile trades at a duration/scarcity premium that a textbook WACC-based Gordon-growth DCF does not capture.
cross_check_memo.note: For reference, applying the current ~24.6x EV/EBITDAFI multiple to Year-10 base-case EBITDAFI (NZ$1,252m) implies an EV of roughly NZ$30.8bn -- multiples of the DCF-derived enterprise value. This illustrates the gap between a cash-flow-discipline valuation and observed market pricing for this asset class; it is not itself a recommended fair-value estimate. Note the underlying EV/EBITDAFI inputs are FY2025 based; FY2026 annual results (due 20-Aug-2026) may shift both the FY2025-vs-FY2026 EBITDAFI base and the multiple once released.

rab_cross_check_memo.description: Regulated asset base (RAB) sanity anchor, alongside the EV/EBITDAFI multiple cross-check, given AIA's dual-till Commerce Commission information-disclosure regime for the aeronautical segment.
rab_cross_check_memo.approach: AIA does not publish a single consolidated RAB figure the way a pure price-cap utility would (its dual-till model mixes a regulated aeronautical asset base with wholly unregulated retail/property/car-park assets), so a precise RAB-multiple cross-check cannot be built from public disclosure alone. As a proxy, book shareholders' equity (NZ$10,582.3m at H1-2026, reflecting substantial capitalised capex already spent on the terminal/airfield programme plus historical investment-property revaluations) provides a floor-level anchor: the current market cap of ~NZ$14,942m (1,705.7m shares x NZ$8.76) implies a P/B of ~1.41x. That premium to book is far smaller than the DCF-implied gap (market cap vs base-case DCF equity value of NZ$3,234m, a ~4.6x multiple) because book value already capitalises the committed capex spend that the DCF has not yet turned into cash flow -- i.e. the market is paying close to book for hard infrastructure assets plus a modest premium for the regulated monopoly franchise, which is a much smaller and more defensible gap than the pure discounted-owner-cash-flow gap.
rab_cross_check_memo.note: This RAB/book-value anchor is a sanity check, not a valuation method in its own right -- it is presented to show the market premium over AIA's regulated/asset-heavy balance sheet is much narrower (P/B ~1.4x, within the historical 1.25-2.11x ex-outlier range in the sanity_check table below) than the premium over the pure owner-FCF DCF, reinforcing that the DCF gap is a duration/terminal-value modelling artefact of the capex supercycle rather than evidence AIA trades at an indefensible multiple of its underlying regulated and physical asset base.

base.note: Because interim FCF (Years 1-8) is deeply negative during the capex supercycle, even the fair-value-consistent 15%-IRR entry price is at or below zero on this model -- i.e. no price today compensates a buyer at a 15% hurdle for absorbing 8 years of cash-negative capex investment ahead of the payoff, at these WACC/terminal-growth settings. This is a direct consequence of the capex trough and should be read alongside the cross-check memo, valuation_philosophy, and rab_cross_check_memo, not in isolation.
base.entry_price_correction_note: Terminal value rebuilt at the hurdle rate 2026-09-01: min(Gordon@hurdle, cap x FCF_N). The superseded value held the WACC-built terminal value and varied only the discounting.

sensitivity.note: Sensitivity built off the BASE-case FCF path (10yr). Rows = WACC (5.5%-9.5%), Columns = terminal growth (1.25%-3.25%). Low-WACC rows are flat because the 20x FCF terminal cap binds rather than Gordon growth. Corrected-SBC recomputation left every cell in this matrix unchanged (SBC is immaterial at ~0.06% of revenue).

sanity_check.basis: SBC-adjusted on both sides (AIA SBC is immaterial, NZ$0.4-0.6m/yr per the corrected series, so adjusted ~= GAAP; these deliberately differ from screener P/E which uses GAAP EPS). Historical multiples use June FY-end closing prices. Outlier years excluded from averages: FY2018 & FY2021 (investment-property revaluation gains inflate earnings), FY2020-FY2023 (COVID border closure and recovery distortion), FY2024 (NZ$5.5m NPAT from the one-off deferred-tax charge after NZ removed building depreciation deductions) - kept in the table for visibility.
sanity_check.note: Check passed in the over-valuation direction it is designed to catch, but the gap runs the OPPOSITE way: base IV NZ$1.90 implies ~6.2x EV/EBITDA vs a 17.8x average (56.8x max) historical trading range. The market persistently pays a duration/scarcity premium for monopoly airport infrastructure that a 7.5% WACC Gordon-growth DCF discounting 5-8 years of negative capex-supercycle FCF cannot reproduce. See cross_check_memo, rab_cross_check_memo, and valuation_philosophy: the DCF says AIA is expensive relative to owner cash flows, not that the model tripped.
